weakness: The pipeline never looked at the space it needed. A movable 18 cm box standing in front of the bottom drawer made the planner refuse every approach to the handle (10/10 seeds: 'no collision-free path'), and nothing in the pipeline could remove it. Repair exposed two hidden weaknesses: the default grasp of a box-shaped obstacle only tried two top-down yaws, both unreachable near the robot's centre line; and the drawer pull was open-loop: on some seeds the gripper slipped off the handle while the hand finished all pull steps 'successfully', the drawer stayed shut, and the object was then dropped in front of the closed drawer.
how_found: Questioned A5 (the space in front of the drawer is free). Real drawers have things parked in front of them, and the pipeline left obstacles entirely to the planner, which can route around an obstacle but never remove it; in front of a drawer there is no way around.
why_missed: In the nominal scene the table in front of the cabinet is empty, so a planner-only strategy and an unverified pull always worked; the slipped-handle case was masked because one noisy grasp in ten happened to hold.
fix: Before touching the handle, compute the volume the drawer and the pulling hand sweep (cabinet face to opening + 25 cm along the pull direction, +-20 cm sideways, table to handle + 15 cm); every non-task obstacle (boxes averaged over 5 get_obstacles calls) overlapping it is picked up (fallback grasp search over 12 top-down yaws and 8 side directions, opening sized to the box) and set down on a free table spot on that arm's side, then the volume is re-checked; an obstacle that cannot be moved is remembered. The pull is now closed-loop: after each 3.5 cm step the handle's travel is measured by detection, and if the grasp is lost or the handle stops following, it is re-grasped where it is (3 attempts); placing is skipped if the drawer is open < 10 cm. The drop orientation turns the finger closing axis along the drawer front so the fingers cannot touch the cabinet face above.
general_rule: Before any motion that needs free space, compute the whole volume the robot and the moved part will sweep and clear movable objects out of it (verifying they left), and close the loop on every contact motion by measuring the manipulated object's own displacement instead of trusting the robot's motion status.

weakness: Every step assumed open space above the work: the pull grasp opened the gripper fully (its upper finger reaches 12 cm above the handle), and the object was always lowered into the drawer from above with a top-down grip. With a fixed board overhanging the drawer 9 cm above the handle, the full-open handle grasp hit the board, the clearing step tried to pick up the board itself, and there was no way to put the object in from above.
how_found: Questioned A5/A9 (the space above the opened drawer is free). Real drawers often sit under a counter or shelf, and every motion in the pipeline came down from above.
why_missed: In the nominal scene nothing is above the drawer, so the default full-open grip and top-down placement were never constrained.
fix: Not recovered in 5 of 6 repairs (best: drawer opened on 3/10 seeds, 0/10 success); variation marked unsolved and the pipeline reverted to round 1. Tried: treat boxes too wide to grip as immovable furniture; a low-profile handle grip (horizontal approach, fingers closing vertically, opening sized to the clearance under the board) searched over 9 approach directions and both wrist rolls; precise handle height from 30 averaged detections; a side grip of the object with the fingers pointing into the drawer and a horizontal insertion between the drawer's front wall and the board. Why it failed: the handle sits ~1.5 cm under the next drawer, so a vertical pinch has a few-mm window (too high and the fingers grip the drawer above), smaller than the remaining perception error; one arm cannot reach under the board at all; and each added step (side pick near the table, insertion through a 7 cm gap) failed often enough that the chain never completed.
general_rule: Before choosing a strategy, compute the clearance envelope each step actually needs (gripper opening, finger length, wrist and forearm) against the space around the target, and if a step's tolerance is smaller than your perception error, change the approach (a different grip, a different arm, or a different place) rather than repeating the same step more precisely.

weakness: The pipeline assumed the drawer always reaches its full travel: it pulled a fixed 17 cm, gave up below 10 cm, and aimed the drop at a fixed 6 cm behind the handle. A fixed low block stopping the drawer after ~9 cm broke every step: the clearing step 'moved' the fixed block with an empty hand (the grip reported holding, the block never rose), the fully open fingers no longer fit between handle and block, the pull retried a hard stop three times, and the pipeline gave up.
how_found: Questioned A3/A10 (the drawer opens to its full travel). Real drawers are often stopped short by clutter, a door or a short runner, and every number in the drop step was a nominal offset, not a measurement.
why_missed: The nominal drawer always opened fully, so fixed thresholds and offsets were never wrong.
fix: Repairs (2 of 6, best 0.2; marked unsolved, pipeline reverted): verify that a grasped obstacle actually rises before carrying it (fixed things are recognised at once); fall back to a partly open handle grip when the full-open grasp has no free path; treat two stalls at the same opening while the handle is still held as a hard stop and continue with that opening; compute the drop point from the measured gap between the drawer's front wall and the cabinet face; drop slowly with contact monitoring when the planner's margin exceeds the real clearance. Why unsolved: with ~9 cm of travel the exposed gap (~7.5 cm) is barely wider than the hand (6.2 cm), and the 6-DoF arms reach the required top-down pose within ~1 cm of the cabinet face only on ~2/10 layouts, so the variation is close to infeasible for this robot (my design error: I did not check reachability before gating it).
general_rule: Treat every action's outcome as a measurement: when a step achieves less than planned (a part stops early, an object does not rise), re-derive the following targets from the measured state and check that they are still reachable with the gripper's real envelope before acting, instead of continuing with nominal offsets or retrying the same step.

weakness: The drawer's opening was measured as the handle's travel in the world from where it was first seen. When the light cabinet slid 12 cm towards the robot while the drawer was being reached for and pulled, the handle's travel counted as opening: the pull stopped with the drawer open only a few cm, and every drop pose was then unreachable (10/10 seeds).
how_found: Questioned A6 (the scene is static). Light furniture moves when a drawer is dragged, and the round-1 progress measurement used a world-fixed reference that assumes the cabinet stays put.
why_missed: The cabinet is fixed in the nominal scene, so the world frame and the cabinet frame coincide and the measurement looked correct; round 1 had just introduced it as the fix for an open-loop pull.
fix: The opening is now the handle's offset from the cabinet body along the pull direction (both re-detected and averaged at every check) minus its closed value, so the pull continues until the drawer is open relative to the cabinet, wherever the cabinet goes. One repair.
general_rule: Measure a manipulation's progress in the frame of the object being manipulated (relative to its own body or base, re-detected each time), never against a world reference recorded earlier, because the supporting object can move while you act on it.

weakness: The drawer was pulled at the planner's normal speed through a friction pinch on a thin handle bar. With stiff runners (damping 60 N s/m) the resisting force exceeded what the pinch could hold: the handle slipped out after a few cm each time, three re-grasps opened the drawer only 5-10 cm, and the drop then failed (2/10). Repair also exposed that reaching for the handle while the cabinet itself was still moving closed the gripper on the cabinet body instead.
how_found: Questioned A3/A8 (the drawer slides easily, so a pinch grip holds). Real drawers stick and drag; the pull speed was never chosen, only inherited from the planner.
why_missed: In the nominal scene the drawer needs almost no force, so speed and grip strength never mattered, and the closed-loop re-grasp from round 1 hid the slips as long as the drawer was free.
fix: Pull at slow speed in 3.5 cm steps (resistance from the runners grows with speed; smaller 1 cm steps were tried and failed because each step's progress drowned in detection noise), allow up to 6 re-grasps from wherever the handle is, and wait until the cabinet and the object are still (two averaged detections 0.5 s apart within 8 mm) before reaching for them. Two repairs; base 1.0, v1 1.0, v5 0.9, v6 1.0.
general_rule: When moving something against resistance, slow down (drag forces grow with speed and a friction grip holds only so much), size each step so its expected progress is well above your measurement noise, re-grasp from the current position whenever the grip slips, and never start a grasp while the target or its support is still moving.

weakness: The pipeline assumed a small object: top-down grasp with the gripper pre-opened to width + 2 cm (capped at full opening), a drop 6-12 cm above an aim point 6 cm behind the handle. Scaled 1.5x, cubes and boxes no longer fit between the fingers (no collision-free grasp), and long objects dropped like that landed across the drawer's front wall or against the cabinet face.
how_found: Questioned A7 (the object is small). Real objects vary in size and the pipeline never compared the object's dimensions with the gripper's capacity or with the size of the opening it is dropped into.
why_missed: All nominal objects are 3-7 cm across, well within the gripper and the drawer gap.
fix: None: marked unsolved without repairs. Three of ten seeds are a rubik's cube that becomes 10 cm on every side, wider than the 9 cm maximum gripper gap; carrying it with both arms would need synchronized dual-arm motion, which the API does not offer. The variation therefore cannot reach 0.8 (my design error: I did not check the scaled sizes against the gripper before gating).
general_rule: Before planning a grasp or a placement, compare the object's measured dimensions with the gripper's maximum opening and with the free space at the destination, and choose the grasp axis, the orientation and the release height from that comparison, declaring the task infeasible for this gripper when no axis fits.

weakness: The pipeline assumed the object stands alone with room for the open fingers on some side; the clearing from round 1 only looked at the drawer's work volume. With the object packed between three blocks (1.6 cm gaps, fingers 3.7 cm thick) every grasp was refused and nothing made room (10/10).
how_found: Questioned A12/A5 at the grasp (the object stands alone). Items in trays and crowded shelves are packed against each other.
why_missed: Round 1 generalised clearing only to the volume the drawer and the pulling hand sweep, not to the volume the fingers need around the object.
fix: Repairs (4 of 6, best 0.3; marked unsolved, pipeline reverted): when no grasp of the object has a free path, move neighbouring movable obstacles away (verifying they rose) and retry; grasp blocks at their free ends, not only at their centre; prefer blocks whose ends stick out past the object; pull the drawer slowly only after a first stall to save time. Found on the way: the stillness check from round 3 compared two 5-sample averages with an 8 mm tolerance, below the noise of their difference, so it waited on still objects for seconds. Why unsolved: freeing a grasp axis needs two block moves (~20-30 s each), and with the drawer sequence this exceeds the 120 s episode budget whenever anything is retried.
general_rule: Before acting on a target, reserve the volume your fingers (not just your arm) need around it and plan which neighbours to move as a whole within the time budget, and set every threshold for 'did it move' well above the noise of the measurement it is compared with.

weakness: Arms were assigned by a fixed rule (object to the arm on its side, drawer to the other). With the cabinet 20 cm to the right, the left arm could not reach the handle or the drop zone, and a right-side object stood in the drawer's path: the opening drawer knocked it off the table.
how_found: Questioned A1/A10 (the cabinet stands in the middle, so each arm reaches its sub-task). Screening showed every other realistic edit left the pipeline >= 0.6; this one dropped it to 0.1.
why_missed: With the cabinet centred, the fixed assignment always gave each arm a reachable sub-task, and the object never lay in the drawer's path.
fix: Repairs (5 of 6, best 0.6; marked unsolved, pipeline reverted): assign each sub-task to the arm nearer to it (possibly one arm for both); if the picking arm cannot reach the drawer, set the object down mid-table for the other arm; move the object itself out of the drawer's path before opening; fall back to the other arm when the nearer one cannot open the drawer, switching at the first table collision instead of re-grasping six times; the noise-robust stillness check from v8 again. Why unsolved: pulling at x = 0.24 the right arm's links strike the table after ~10 cm (2-4 kN) and the drawer springs back shut, while the left arm cannot reach the handle; this is the robot's reach and the simulator/planner behaviour at its edge, not something the pipeline can change.
general_rule: Assign each sub-task to the effector that can actually reach it (one effector may do several in sequence, or hand the object over through a free spot), treat the manipulated object itself as an obstacle to other sub-tasks, and switch effector or strategy at the first sign of a kinematic limit instead of retrying with the same one.

weakness: Same scene as unsolved v9 (cabinet 20 cm right), retried after backend v2 stopped the arm from grinding on the table. With the fixed rule 'drawer to the arm opposite the object', the far arm could not reach the handle; the near arm, gripping the bar at its centre far out to the side, pulled with a cramped wrist that sagged 6 cm into the table and slipped off the handle; a right-side object lay in the drawer's path; and a blocked retreat left the hand where going home swept the half-open drawer shut.
how_found: Questioned A1/A10 (each arm can reach its sub-task). Screening showed this was the only realistic edit that still broke the round-3 pipeline; v9 had been abandoned at 0.6 because of the table-grinding backend bug.
why_missed: With the cabinet centred both arms reach the handle comfortably, so nearness and fixed roles were never questioned and the grip point on the handle bar never mattered.
fix: Four repairs on top of the v9 attempt (backend v2 throughout; v2d widened the force-limit release window for a hand pressed on the table to 0.4 s): sub-tasks go to the arm that reaches them, but for a handle far to one side the arm reaching across from the other side pulls (observed to track the pull cleanly where the near arm sags); the bar is gripped 6 cm from its centre towards the robot's centre line with a partly open, vertically closing grip; after a stall the pull continues in free-path slow steps; after letting go the hand lifts clear before backing off; the object is moved out of the drawer's path first if needed; and if the picking arm cannot reach the drawer it sets the object down mid-table for the other arm. Final: base 1.0, v1 0.9, v5 0.8, v6 0.9, v10 0.8.
general_rule: Choose the effector and the grip point for a forceful motion by how well the arm can carry it out there (a comfortable, uncramped configuration, observed from how it tracks), not by which effector is nearest or which grip point is nominal, and move clear of a just-released moving part before travelling so the travel cannot undo the work.

weakness: Every pick came straight down on the object and lifted straight up. A fixed shelf 1 cm above the tallest object made every top-down grasp unreachable (10/10).
how_found: Questioned A9/A5 at the pick (the space above the object is free). Objects on shelves and under counters are common.
why_missed: Nothing in the nominal scene is above the object.
fix: Repairs (2 of 6, best 0.0; marked unsolved, pipeline reverted): detect an overhang above the object and pick from the side (fingers pointing away from the robot, opening sized to the object), draw the object out horizontally until clear, then lift; then pitch the approach 17-34 deg downward so the fingertips reach low objects while the wrist stays high and behind. Why unsolved: the free height under the shelf (11 cm) is about the height of the hand's wrist link, so approaches that reach the object put the wrist on the table (100-560 N, stopped by the force limit) or are unreachable, and 2-3 cm objects cannot be gripped from the side at all.
general_rule: Check the full hand envelope (wrist included, not just the fingers) against the free space around the target before choosing a grasp, and when no grasp fits, move the target first by non-prehensile means (drag it into the open) instead of forcing a grasp in place.

weakness: The pick assumed nothing rests on or leans against the object. With a light board lying on it, top-down grasps of the object were blocked and side grasps pushed the board and the cube; 7/10 failed.
how_found: Questioned A12/A5 at the pick (nothing rests on the object). Items covered by a lid, a sheet or another item are common, and screening showed it was the one remaining realistic edit that broke the round-4 pipeline (0.1).
why_missed: Nothing ever rested on the object in the nominal scene or in earlier variations.
fix: Repairs (5 of 6, best 0.5; marked unsolved, pipeline reverted): detect things resting on the object (bottom at its top, overlapping it) and take them off before the pick, set down >= 20 cm away; grip the lid from above only, first with the fingertips just above the object (too weak: it dragged the lid off sideways), then at the lid's mid-height with a slow straight lift; also clear anything left leaning against the object. A control without the lid scored 1.0. Why unsolved: the object is a 10 g cube; every slip of the lid or graze of a fingertip during removal makes the simulator fling it off the table (metres away), and the extra removal step pushes other seeds over the 120 s budget. Controls: the same cube and pose without the lid scored 1.0, and with the object at a realistic 200 g the frozen round-4 pipeline already scored 0.7 under the lid (it does not break). So v12's break, and its failure to recover, measured mostly the simulator's handling of a 10 g object under contact, not a robustness gap of the program.
general_rule: Before grasping, check what rests on or leans against the target and remove it with a firm grip and a straight, slow lift, then verify both that it is gone and that the target did not move, because a half-removed cover that slides off becomes an obstacle pressed against the target.
